description_full: Equifax Inc. operates as a data, analytics, and technology company. The company operates through three segments: Workforce Solutions, U.S. Information Solutions (USIS), and International. The Workforce Solutions segment offers services that enables customers to verify income, employment, educational history, criminal justice data, healthcare professional licensure, and sanctions of people in the United States; and employer customers with services that assist them in complying with and automating certain payroll-related and human resource management processes throughout the entire cycle of the employment relationship. The U.S. Information Solutions segment provides consumer and commercial information services, such as credit information and credit scoring, credit modeling and portfolio analytics, locate, fraud detection and prevention, identity verification, and other consulting services; mortgage services; financial marketing services; identity management services; and credit monitoring products. The International segment offers information service products, which include consumer and commercial services comprising credit and financial information, and credit scoring and modeling; and credit and other marketing products and services, as well as information, technology, and services to support debt collections and recovery management. The company also provides information solutions for businesses, governments and consumers; and human resources business process automation and outsourcing services for employers. It operates in Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Honduras, India, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand, Paraguay, Peru, Portugal, Spain, the United Kingdom, Uruguay, and the United States. The company was founded in 1899 and is headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia.

financial_summary: Equifax, Inc. is a large-cap industrials business with a $22.3B market cap on $6.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $1.1B in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.45× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -8.1% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.7× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 5.2×.

Management returns a meaningful 5.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 18% operating margin runs 9pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.64x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-1.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 29% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 11% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 17% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 41% and a beta of 1.18, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.32 vs 5y 1.24), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $245.3M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 36% in the 2020 crash, 47% in the 2022 bear market and 50% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $173 (margin of safety -9%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 24%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $105 to $280 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 30.7 vs 23.3 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-10%).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 20 covering analysts target $200 on average, 6% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.3%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.48).
It converts 19% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 2.45x, but high accruals (-8.1% of assets).
ROE of 14% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.6x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.3% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.7x net debt to EBITDA ($180.8M of cash against $5.1B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 5.2x.
The current ratio of 0.60 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 57% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.8% over 3 years, 8.0% over 5 years and 8.6% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 16.7% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 1% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 12%.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (7.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 25, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.6%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (20 sales, net $22.5M sold).
It returns 5.2% a year to shareholders (4.2% in buybacks and 1.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 38 consecutive years, raising it 4.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 15,000 employees, each generates about $405K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 8.2% a year.
That works out to $76K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.0M (12x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
